learn.intro: How did Hitler turn his position as Chancellor into a dictatorship, how did the Nazis control Germany, and how did their policies affect young people, women, the Churches, Jews and workers?

sections.title: 1. Setting up the dictatorship

blocks.p: The Reichstag Fire (27 February 1933): a Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was arrested. Hitler claimed a communist plot; Hindenburg signed an emergency decree suspending civil rights, and thousands of communists were arrested before the March election.

The Enabling Act (23 March 1933) gave Hitler the power to make laws without the Reichstag for four years. Communist deputies were banned and the SA intimidated others. Trade unions were banned in May 1933 and by July 1933 the Nazis were the only legal party.

The Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934): Hitler had Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders, plus political rivals, killed by the SS. The SA, which had over 2 million members, had threatened the army and wanted a 'second revolution'. The army was reassured.
When Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler combined the posts of Chancellor and President as Führer. The army swore an oath of personal loyalty to him.

evidence: 30 June 1934: Night of the Long Knives.

blocks.p: The police state: the SS, led by Heinrich Himmler, and the Gestapo (secret police) arrested opponents; informers reported on neighbours; concentration camps such as Dachau (1933) held political prisoners; judges had to follow Nazi ideas.

Propaganda and censorship: Joseph Goebbels controlled newspapers, radio, films, books and art. Cheap radios spread Hitler's speeches; huge rallies at Nuremberg showed Nazi power; books by Jewish or 'un-German' writers were burned in 1933; the 1936 Berlin Olympics showed off Germany.

How successful? There was little open opposition, but some continued: Pastor Martin Niemöller and the Confessing Church, some young people who rejected the Hitler Youth, and underground communist and socialist groups. Many Germans conformed through fear, while others supported the regime because it brought jobs and order.

sections.title: 3. Young people, education, women and the Churches

blocks.p: Young people: boys joined the Hitler Youth and girls the League of German Maidens, with camping, sport, marching and Nazi ideas. By 1939 8 million young people were members, and membership became compulsory in 1939. In schools, teachers had to join the Nazi Teachers' League; subjects such as history and biology taught Nazi ideas about race.

Women: the Nazis wanted women to focus on 'children, kitchen, church'. Marriage loans encouraged women to leave work and have children; the Mother's Cross rewarded large families; women were removed from jobs such as doctors, lawyers and civil servants.

The Churches: Hitler signed a Concordat with the Pope in 1933, promising not to interfere with the Catholic Church, but later broke it. The Nazis set up a Reich Church for Protestants; Pastor Niemöller's Confessing Church opposed it, and Niemöller was sent to a concentration camp.

evidence: 8 million young people in Nazi youth groups by 1939.

sections.title: 4. Racial policy and the persecution of Jews

blocks.p: The Nazis believed in an 'Aryan' master race and treated Jews as enemies. Persecution increased step by step:

ul: April 1933: a boycott of Jewish shops; Jews dismissed from the civil service.
September 1935: the Nuremberg Laws took away Jews' German citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews.

9–10 November 1938: Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass') — synagogues, shops and homes attacked; around 100 Jews killed and about 30,000 Jewish men sent to concentration camps. Jews were then fined 1 billion marks.

blocks.p: When Hitler came to power 6 million Germans were unemployed; by 1939 this was reduced to about half a million. Methods: the National Labour Service (RAD) gave young men work on projects such as autobahns; rearmament created jobs in factories; conscription (from 1935) took nearly 1 million men into the armed forces; and women and Jews dismissed from jobs were not counted ('invisible unemployment').

Trade unions were replaced by the German Labour Front (DAF), which controlled wages and hours. Strength Through Joy (KdF) offered cheap holidays, concerts and sport, and a scheme to save for a Volkswagen 'people's car'. Workers had jobs, but longer hours and no right to strike.

misconceptions.right: Some did — Niemöller, the Confessing Church and some young people — but opposition was small and dangerous.

misconceptions.wrong: All unemployed people got real jobs.
misconceptions.right: Women and Jews removed from work were simply not counted.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of the fall in unemployment.
evidence.model: Unemployment fell from 6 million in 1933 to about half a million by 1939.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of increasing persecution of Jews.
evidence.model: April 1933 boycott; Nuremberg Laws (1935); Kristallnacht (November 1938), with about 30,000 Jewish men sent to camps.

flashcards.q: How did Hitler use the Reichstag Fire?
flashcards.a: Claimed a communist plot; emergency decree suspended civil rights; thousands of communists arrested.
Hitler became Führer (Chancellor and President); the army swore loyalty to him.

flashcards.q: Name three parts of the Nazi police state.
flashcards.a: SS, Gestapo, concentration camps, informers, Nazi-controlled courts.
Radio, Nuremberg rallies, films, posters, book burning, the 1936 Olympics.

flashcards.q: How did the Nazis control education?
flashcards.a: Teachers joined the Nazi Teachers' League; the curriculum taught Nazi race ideas; Hitler Youth outside school.

flashcards.q: What did the Nazis expect of women?
flashcards.a: Children, kitchen, church — marry, have children and stay at home.
Attacks on synagogues, shops and homes; around 100 Jews killed; about 30,000 men to camps; a 1 billion mark fine on Jews.

flashcards.q: How did the Nazis reduce unemployment?
flashcards.a: Labour Service (autobahns), rearmament, conscription, and not counting women and Jews.

checklist.text: I can describe how Hitler set up the dictatorship (Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act, Night of the Long Knives, Führer).
I can judge how successful Nazi methods of control were (police state, censorship, propaganda).
I can explain Nazi policies towards education, women, young people and the Churches and their impact.
I can explain Nazi racial policy and the increasing persecution of Jews.
I can explain policies to reduce unemployment, the Labour Service, the Labour Front and Strength Through Joy.
